title: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving
hook: the Forgiving, again and again, however often you return

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Musawwir: the Fashioner who shaped every face, and who looks at hearts, not forms. Your line was every face shaped. Did you catch a first judgment and set it down? Day two hundred forty-four.

Everyone has one. The same old thing. The temper that flares at the same person. The habit you've quit eleven times. The promise to yourself you break every Tuesday. The first time, you ask for forgiveness sincerely. The fifth time, it feels a little embarrassing. By the twentieth, you stop asking, because surely there's a limit, and surely you've hit it. You'd be tired of you. Anyone would. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told a story about exactly this person, a servant who does the same wrong, again and again, and keeps coming back. Bukhari and Muslim both record it. And the answer is a name built for repetition. Today: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving.
screen: `THE SAME OLD THING.` → `THE TWENTIETH TIME.` → `SURELY THERE'S A LIMIT?`

segments.voice: In the story, a servant commits a sin and says: my Lord, I have sinned, forgive me. And Allah says: My servant knew that he has a Lord who forgives sins and holds to account for them. I have forgiven My servant. Time passes. The servant does it again. The same words: my Lord, I sinned, forgive me. The same answer: forgiven. A third time. The same. Scholars explain the story carefully: it isn't permission to do wrong. It's about the one who keeps sincerely turning back, meaning it each time. For that person, the door doesn't close. The root of the name is gh-f-r, to cover. A mighfar is a helmet, the thing that covers the head and protects it in battle. So forgiveness, maghfirah, is more than a pardon. It's a covering: the wrong is covered over, and you're protected from its harm. Arabic has three names from this root. Al-Ghafir, the one who forgives. Al-Ghafur, whose forgiveness is great. And al-Ghaffar, built on a form that means again and again, over and over, as often as it's needed. Al-Ghaffar is the name for the twentieth time. The prophet Nuh told his people: ask your Lord for forgiveness; He is ever Ghaffar. And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that he himself asked Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day. If the one closest to Allah asked seventy times, no one needs to be embarrassed at the fifth. Astaghfirullah: I ask Allah's forgiveness. It's one of the most repeated words a Muslim says.
screen: `THE SERVANT WHO KEEPS RETURNING.` · `GH-F-R — TO COVER, LIKE A HELMET.` · `GHAFIR, GHAFUR, GHAFFAR.` · `SEVENTY TIMES A DAY.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your same old thing come to mind. Don't flinch from it and don't argue for it. Just look at it honestly, the way you'd look at a scrape on your knee. Notice any tiredness, any shame. Now picture it being covered, gently, like a helmet over a head, or a blanket over someone sleeping. Breathe under that covering. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, once, slowly, and mean it, even if you've said it for this a hundred times before. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ghaffar. The Forgiving, again and again: the one who covers wrongs as often as a person sincerely returns. Today's word.
Your line: forgiven again. Today, when the same old thing happens, don't give up on yourself. Turn back once more, and if you pray, ask again. Day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims say astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness, many times a day: after each prayer (often three times), at small slips, and in longer forms like sayyid al-istighfar, following the Prophet's practice of seeking forgiveness more than seventy times a day.

fork.setup: the servant sins, asks forgiveness, is forgiven, and does it again. he asks a second time. what happens?
options: he's told he's used up his chance
fork.reveal: forgiven again, and a third time: My servant knew he has a Lord who forgives (Bukhari; Muslim).

original.note: Arabic: the Forgiving, again and again; from gh-f-r, to cover.

trapdoor: what you thought: God forgives, up to a point.
what it means: the one who covers wrongs over and over, as often as a person sincerely returns.
what a scholar hears: the fa''al form marks repetition; mighfar, helmet; Bukhari 7507 and Muslim 2758, the returning servant; 71:10, Nuh; Bukhari 6307, seventy times.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7507; Sahih Muslim 2758 (the servant who sins and returns)
Qur'an 71:10 (Nuh: ask forgiveness of your Lord, He is ever Forgiving)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6307 (more than seventy times a day)
Qur'an 20:82 (I am Ghaffar to the one who repents, believes and does good)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 7507, 6307; Muslim 2758) cited from memory; confirm.
The hadith ends in some wordings with 'do what you will, I have forgiven you'; the script omits that line and gives the scholars' explanation to avoid misreading.
Mighfar (helmet) as a gh-f-r word is standard; confirm the covering explanation of maghfirah.
